text: These comments are for "Newtons Fruit Thins - Cranberry Citrus Oat" sold by Nabisco. The package states "crispy cookies" think the firmness and thickness of a graham cracker - yes that firm. These 3-inch round wafers come in a rigid plastic tray that slides into a foil-lined package. Nonetheless several cookies in the two packages I sampled were broken into several large pieces upon opening. Probably not typical but that's what I observed. I found the cookies brittle; they had a tendency to break into several pieces after a bite. As an adult I could compensate be adjusting my method of holding the wafer but children will have a problem. The cranberry citrus oat had a pleasant flavor with a hit of citrus. The package state "made with real fruit" therefore what you have are many small pieces of dried cranberries throughout the cookie. I like cranberries but after they are dried and baked they become semi-hard and chewy and tend to stick to your teeth. I was somewhat taken back by the work "Newtons" in large letters on the package. My understanding of this term is of a soft chewy fruit filled cookie like a fig or apple Newton. I do not see the connection then again I am not in Sales or Marketing where these decisions are made.
label: negative

text: My puppy is teething so I had previously purchased the original Nylabone made out of flavored plastic. When she finally finished the original plastic bone I decided to go back to the store and grab some more. I was looking around and came across these, "natural," flavored bones and thought.... "SWEET!!! Same great bone but easier to digest!" How wrong I was. First off this is NOTHING like the plastic teething bones. They crumble easily... and by easily I mean my 3.5 month old Wheaten Terrier destroyed these in less than 30min, and she's only about 15 pounds right now. They are recommended for dogs 6 months + with pretty much a full set of permanent teeth because they can shred the bone more easily and to a finer debris. For my dog this was BS... she destroyed these into tiny little flakes that can be easily digested AND managed to get them all over her underbelly and tangled in her fur. The mess wasn't an issue.. the durability was. This is basically an expensive treat, I much rather give her bullysticks over this as a treat (and they last longer). If your dog is teething, this is def NOT the Nylabone version you want. Stick to the original plastic flavored bones or frozen towels. Both work great.

Wolfberry has its own benefits (not nearly those of Goji IMO), but for Wolfberries these are widly overpriced. You can get the same in Chinese stores for probably closer to $10 for twice the amount. With the dollar devaluation top quality Goji berries have gotten very expensive for regular use. So if you're looking for cheaper alternatives like I was here, look elsewhere. Check out some of the cheap goji berries (that are in fact wolfberries and usually say so) on Ebay from Chinese sources. They'll be quite a bit cheaper and likely quite a bit fresher.

text: Ask a Chinese friend about "forbidden rice" (禁米), unless they are history buff like myself, they will give you a puzzled look. The story about emperor depriving commoners of red rice is a hoax made in America, like the legion of fortune cookies. Most fortune cookies are made in a wholesome factory near Atlanta. We trust that fortune cookies are safe to eat. "Forbidden rice?" There is a red rice in China, dark red, close to red bean. The color varies from gran to gran. Its thick bran provides a pleasant nutty flavor and al dente texture. The color does not come off easily. You can get them from Chinese grocery store. What is sold as "forbidden rice" at Amazon and Costco has a uniformed black to deep purple color. It appears to be rice over-milled, dyed, and polished. Drop a few grains in water, you can see color coming off. And the color tent to sink to the bottom. That is a easy tell tail. When cooked, the favor and texture of bran are absent. If they use red rice, they have milled away its bran to make the rice easy to dye. There is nothing wrong with using food coloring. But is the ink FDA approved? We do not know. The label does not say. I am returning mine to Costco. I will ask Costco to pull it off the shelf.

I was somewhat annoyed as the tin doesn't say much of anything that is helpful, but what I eventually tried was cutting the excess portion of the wrapper off so that it looked exactly like a Starbucks pod. It worked perfectly and produced a great shot with lots of crema. I am drinking my latte now, and while it is good, I wouldn't say it is any better than my normal Starbucks-pod lattes. As the Starbucks pods are much cheaper (and easier), I'll be sticking with those after this tin.
label: neutral

text: I was very excited to find a cola syrup that was not artificially sweetened, and did not have high fructose corn syrup in it. As for the seller, delivery was prompt and price was reasonable. I definitely appreciate the seller's part of this, but I must say, the product is so-so. It has a different taste to it; and is not an authentic cola taste. For some reason, the taste seems to almost rob the cola of its carbonation. That said, it is not super sweet, which is nice; and, it has no awful after-taste. I don't think I would buy this product again; it depends what other naturally flavored colas I find out there.
label: neutral
